vignette:
At thirty-five, he makes his living as a musician, playing guitar in clubs, recording sessions when they come, and teaching a few students in the afternoons. Before the accident, he talks about his life in terms of sound and movement. He is married, close with his family, and proud of the way he has built something steady out of a career that often feels uncertain. He describes himself then as someone who is always in motion-loading equipment into the car after midnight, driving home on dark highways, humming melodies into his phone so he does not lose them before morning.

The accident happens after a late gig about a year ago. He has packed up his amplifier and guitar and is driving home alone on a wet road just outside the city. He remembers being tired but alert, the windshield wipers moving fast, the red glow of brake lights ahead. Then traffic slows abruptly. He hits the brakes, feels the car skid, and in the next instant hears what he still calls "the explosion," the violent metal-on-metal crash from behind that throws his car forward. He remembers the steering wheel slamming into his chest, glass breaking, the smell of something burning. For a few seconds he is sure he is going to die. He cannot get the driver's door open. He tries to move and feels sharp pain shoot through his shoulder and ribs. What stays with him most is the trapped feeling-his breath coming fast, the seat belt locked tight, the sound of horns and rain and somebody shouting from outside the car.

He survives with injuries that heal better on paper than they do in his mind. In the first weeks afterward, he tells himself he is lucky. His wife helps him shower and dress while his bruises fade. Friends from the music scene send messages and cover a few gigs for him. He expects that once his body recovers, he will go back to normal.

Instead, the accident keeps happening. It returns when he closes his eyes at night: the headlights in the mirror, the jolt, the certainty that impact is coming. He wakes suddenly drenched in sweat, heart pounding so hard he sits on the edge of the bed pressing a hand to his chest. Sometimes his wife reaches for him and he flinches before he knows where he is. He starts staying up later because he dreads sleep, scrolling on his phone or playing muted chords on an unplugged guitar in the living room.

During the day, he notices himself scanning constantly. In traffic he grips the door handle and checks the rearview mirror over and over. If a car comes up too fast behind him, his whole body tenses. He stops driving on highways first, then at night, then almost altogether unless he has no other choice. When his wife offers to drive, he feels ashamed of how relieved he is. He begins turning down gigs that would require travel, especially if rain is in the forecast. He tells other musicians he is busy or not feeling well. The excuses come easier than explaining why a simple ride across town can leave him shaky and nauseated.

Music, which had always been the place he felt most at ease, changes too. Loud percussive sounds make him jump. At one rehearsal, the drummer drops a stand and the crack of metal on the floor sends him instantly back into the car; his chest tightens, and for a moment he cannot hear what anyone is saying. He laughs it off, steps outside, and vomits in the alley. After that, he becomes more guarded in sessions, sitting near exits, asking without asking for breaks, watching everyone's reactions in case they have noticed.

His wife tells him he is no longer fully with her. He knows what she means. He is irritable in ways that surprise him. Small frustrations-a late payment, a neighbor's car alarm, a text arriving while he is trying to rest-ignite anger that feels too big for the moment. Then just as quickly it collapses into guilt. He misses family gatherings because he does not want to answer questions. He avoids talking about the accident with his parents because his mother cries, and he cannot bear the look on his father's face. At home he moves through rooms checking windows and locks before bed, though he knows the accident did not happen there. Safety has become something he no longer trusts.

He also speaks about a quieter change, one that troubles him more than the fear. He says he used to feel open-toward music, toward people, toward plans. Now he often feels cut off, as if part of him is still trapped in that car, waiting for impact. He can still play beautifully, sometimes automatically, his hands remembering what his mind cannot settle into. Audiences applaud, friends tell him it is good to see him back, and from the outside he appears to be recovering. But he describes going home after performances with his jaw aching from tension, exhausted from pretending to be relaxed. In the present, his world has narrowed around avoiding reminders, enduring sleep in fragments, and trying to protect the life he had before the crash from a fear that keeps insisting the danger has not passed.
